blocks.title: Read history as changing constraints
paragraphs: Computer history is useful when an invention explains a change in what machines could do. Connect a development to its physical implementation, programmability, reliability or cost; a list of names alone does not explain its significance.

This lesson uses a broad sequence of mechanisms. It does not claim exact lecture dates, priority disputes or an exhaustive list of named machines: the normalized academic pack does not contain that detail.

blocks.title: From moving parts to electronic switching
paragraphs: Mechanical calculation represents and changes information through physical motion. Electronic switching replaces that motion with electrical state changes, allowing a different scale of switching speed. Vacuum tubes were an early electronic switching technology.

Transistors provided a smaller solid-state switching element. Relate this change to practical constraints such as component size, power and reliability; do not turn it into a claim that every later machine was faster on every task.

blocks.title: The program becomes stored information
paragraphs: A stored-program machine represents instructions in memory and fetches them for execution. Changing a program can then change the sequence of operations without physically rewiring that sequence.

Distinguish this organizational idea from the technology used to build the switches. Stored programs, transistors and integrated circuits answer different questions: how execution is specified, how a switch is built, and how components are combined.

blocks.title: Integration changes the scale of the machine
paragraphs: Integrated circuits combine multiple electronic components on a chip. Increasing integration reduces the need to assemble each logic element separately and makes larger systems practical within tighter size and cost constraints.

A microprocessor integrates CPU functions on a chip. It is a processor, not automatically the whole computer: memory and I/O still have roles. Moving from individual devices toward integrated processors is a useful technology sequence; organizational ideas can span several such generations.

blocks.title: Turn a milestone into an explanation
paragraphs: Use three parts: identify the development; state which previous constraint it changes; connect that change to computer organization or practical performance. For example, a stored program changes how a sequence of operations is specified, while a transistor changes its physical switching implementation.

When comparing generations, hold the question fixed. A statement about density is not yet a measured execution-time comparison. Consult the original history lecture for its exact named-machine chronology.

blocks.title: Separate technology from organization
paragraphs: Recall the broad development from mechanical mechanisms to electronic switching, transistors, integrated circuits and integrated processors. Explain stored programs as an organizational change rather than another transistor type.
Use the cards to recall the distinctions, then write the unscored explanation in Practice. Historical explanation is reviewed with criteria rather than keyword scoring.

cards.prompt: What changed when calculation moved from mechanical motion to electronic switching?
cards.answer: The physical mechanism for changing state changed. Explain the implications for switching speed and practical construction, rather than treating the change as only a new machine name.

cards.prompt: Why is the stored-program idea different from the invention of a transistor?
cards.answer: A stored program describes how instructions are represented and fetched. A transistor describes a physical switching device; the organizational idea and device technology are separate.

cards.prompt: What is the distinction between an integrated circuit and a complete computer?
cards.answer: An integrated circuit combines components on a chip. A computer still needs organized processing, memory and I/O; a microprocessor integrates CPU functions but need not include the whole system.

guided.title: Explain a development
guided.prompt: Compare the significance of stored programs and increased circuit integration without claiming they are the same kind of change.
rubric: Identify stored instructions and the ability to change an operation sequence without rewiring it.
Explain integration as combining electronic components and changing construction, size or cost constraints.
Keep device technology, organization and a measured performance claim distinct. Several explanations can satisfy these criteria; no automatic score is assigned.
